title: Wound Care & Dressing Change
summary: Assessing and redressing a wound to promote healing and prevent infection.
steps: Review orders for specific wound care instructions. Perform hand hygiene.
Gather all supplies and set up sterile field if required.
Don clean gloves. Gently remove old dressing, noting type, amount, color, and odor of drainage.
Dispose of soiled dressing in biohazard bag. Remove gloves and perform hand hygiene.
Don sterile gloves. Assess the wound — note size (length × width × depth), wound bed color, surrounding skin, and signs of infection.
Irrigate the wound with normal saline or prescribed cleanser. Use a 35mL syringe with 18g angiocath for 8psi irrigation if appropriate.
Pat the periwound skin dry with sterile gauze.
Apply appropriate dressing per wound type and provider order.
Secure dressing with tape or other appropriate method.
Remove gloves and perform hand hygiene.
Document wound assessment including size, color, drainage, odor, periwound skin, and patient tolerance.
nursing_considerations: Obtain a wound culture before cleaning if infection is suspected.
Use Sterile technique for surgical wounds and clean technique for chronic wounds (per facility policy).
Stage pressure injuries (I–IV) and document accurately.
Refer to wound care specialist for non-healing wounds or wounds requiring debridement.
Assess patient pain before, during, and after the procedure.

title: Suture & Staple Removal
summary: Removing sutures or staples from a healed surgical or laceration wound.
equipment: Suture removal kit (iris scissors + tissue forceps) OR staple remover
steps: Verify provider order specifying partial or full removal, and any site-specific instructions.
Explain procedure to patient. Perform hand hygiene and don gloves.
Remove old dressing. Assess wound: approximation, signs of healing, absence of infection.
Clean wound gently with NS-moistened gauze if needed.

For sutures: Grasp the knot with forceps. Slide one blade of iris scissors under the suture adjacent to the knot. Cut and pull the suture through the skin in one smooth motion — pulling toward the wound, not away.
For staples: Position the staple remover under the staple so the lower jaw is centered. Squeeze handles to deform and lift the staple out in one motion.
Place each removed suture/staple on gauze for counting — verify all are removed.
Assess wound after removal — confirm edges remain well-approximated.
Apply Steri-strips if ordered or wound edges appear slightly gapped for additional support.
Cover with a light dressing if wound is not fully epithelialized.
Document number of sutures/staples removed, wound appearance, and patient tolerance.
nursing_considerations: General healing timelines: face 3–5 days, scalp 7–10 days, trunk/extremities 7–14 days, joints 14 days.
Never remove sutures from a wound that shows signs of infection (dehiscence risk) — notify provider.
Always pull the suture toward the wound — pulling away can reopen the healing tissue.
If wound gapes during removal, stop and notify provider before removing remaining sutures.
Instruct patient to protect the wound from sun exposure for 6–12 months to minimize scarring.

title: Pressure Injury Prevention & Staging
summary: Assessing, staging, and documenting pressure injuries, and implementing prevention strategies.
equipment: Pressure-redistributing support surfaces (foam mattress, heel protectors, wedge pillows)
steps: Perform a skin assessment on admission and per facility protocol (typically every shift).
Identify high-risk patients using a validated scale (Braden Scale: scores ≤18 indicate risk).
Inspect bony prominences: sacrum, coccyx, heels, trochanters, elbows, occiput, scapulae.
Stage any identified pressure injury:
Stage 1: Non-blanchable erythema of intact skin.
Stage 2: Partial-thickness skin loss — shallow open ulcer or intact/ruptured blister.
Stage 3: Full-thickness skin loss — subcutaneous fat may be visible.
Stage 4: Full-thickness tissue loss — exposed bone, tendon, or muscle.
Unstageable: Full-thickness loss, wound base obscured by slough or eschar.
Deep Tissue Injury (DTI): Persistent non-blanchable deep red/maroon discoloration or blood-filled blister.
Measure wound dimensions (length × width × depth). Assess wound bed, drainage, periwound skin.
Implement prevention: reposition every 2 hours, use pressure-redistributing surfaces, keep skin clean/dry.
Off-load heels completely — use heel suspension boots or pillows under calves.
Apply moisture barrier cream to areas exposed to incontinence.
Document staging, measurements, and prevention interventions in care plan.
nursing_considerations: Heels and sacrum are the most common pressure injury sites — prioritize off-loading these areas.
Never massage reddened areas over bony prominences — it increases tissue damage.
Incontinence-associated dermatitis (IAD) can mimic or worsen pressure injuries — treat moisture separately.
Stage a pressure injury based on what is visible — do not reverse-stage as it heals.
Pressure injuries are largely preventable — document interventions as evidence of proactive care.

title: Negative Pressure Wound Therapy (NPWT)
summary: Applying and managing a vacuum-assisted closure (VAC) device to promote wound healing.
steps: Verify order including pressure setting (commonly -75 to -125 mmHg) and foam/gauze type.
Perform hand hygiene. Prepare supplies. Explain procedure to patient — offer analgesia 30 minutes prior.
Don gloves. Remove old NPWT dressing. Note foam color, wound drainage, and odor.
Perform wound assessment and measurement. Irrigate wound with NS per order.
Dry the periwound skin thoroughly — NPWT dressing will not seal over moist skin.
Apply skin barrier/prep to periwound area if ordered to protect fragile skin.
Cut foam to fit the wound bed contours. Do NOT pack foam into tunnels/tracts unless specifically ordered.
Place foam into wound. Count and record number of foam pieces used.
Cut transparent drape to cover the foam and extend at least 3–5 cm onto intact periwound skin. Apply smoothly.
Cut a small hole (2–3 cm) in the center of the drape. Apply the SensaT.R.A.C. pad or tubing connector.
Connect tubing to NPWT unit. Insert canister. Turn on device and confirm negative pressure achieved (dressing should collapse).
Set ordered pressure and therapy mode (continuous vs. intermittent) per provider order.
Document wound assessment, foam count, pressure settings, drainage amount/characteristics.
nursing_considerations: Never place NPWT over exposed vessels, nerves, anastomotic sites, or malignant wounds.
Alarm troubleshooting: check for air leaks (press around edges of drape), ensure canister is not full, confirm tubing is not kinked.
Change dressing every 48–72 hours or per order — foam should NOT be left in wound longer than 72 hours.
Always count foam pieces in and out — retained foam is a serious complication.
Discontinue and notify provider if signs of bleeding (bright red drainage, increasing drainage >10x baseline) appear.
